answers.text: The brief says only that a person always makes forward moves. It does not name the person, the interface or the command, and no other file in the plan defines it. The plan does fix what the approval must carry: the record version the person saw. The controller applies the move only if that version still matches.

The brief says the rollout controller is still to be written, so no process exists yet. How often it runs is not stated. The plan says what the controller does (apply mode changes, update counters, run the automatic trigger). It does not set a schedule.

The brief gives the 2 percent threshold and the 10-minute window. It does not say what counts as a charge failure (a declined card or a provider error) or where the charge results come from. The plan does not decide this.

The brief says that in both, the new engine charges and writes the ledger. So the new engine's invoice is the one charged, and the mode decides it. The old engine's invoice goes to the shadow store and is compared with the new one per customer. A mismatch is a total that differs by more than one cent, and the comparison continues in both.

Freeze is my design choice, not something the brief states. The plan sets a freeze flag in the rollout record. Both engines read it before each charge. I did not use billing_mode, because the brief fixes that flag to the four modes. The flag mechanism is still a proposal and is listed in the open questions.

The key is the pair (customer, billing period). The ledger allows one row per key, and the same key is sent to the provider as its idempotency key, so a repeated request cannot charge twice. A ledger intent is a row with that key, marked pending, written before the charge. Recording the result sets the row to succeeded or failed and stores the provider's reference. The brief does not define the row's fields, so the plan leaves them to the build.

A period is already charged when the ledger has a succeeded row for its key. A period is due and uncharged when its due date has passed under the existing billing terms and it has no succeeded row. For a ledger intent with no result, reconcile queries the provider by the key. If the provider shows a charge, reconcile records it as succeeded. If not, the period is uncharged. The plan now says this in reconcile step 3.

The brief says that after a rollback the rollout goes through shadow again and the 7-day count starts over. So a restart is old_only, then shadow, then both, through the normal forward moves. What happens to the shadow data after a rollback is not in the brief. It is listed as an open question.

Resume charges only periods with no succeeded ledger row under the key. A period the new engine already charged has that row, so the old engine skips it, whatever amount the old engine would compute. The check is on the ledger row, not on the amount.

questions.text: In resume, if the old engine's charge comes back failed (for example a declined card), what happens to that period? Is it retried, and does it count as 'done' so rollback can finish?
questions.about: Resume: records the result as succeeded or failed

questions.text: If a rollback from new_only is still in RollingBack when day 35 arrives, does the state lock, or does the rollback continue? Does the 35-day clock stop?
questions.about: new_only --> new_only_locked: day 35 in new_only reached with no rollback

questions.about: both --> new_only: no unresolved mismatches

questions.about: Freeze: stop all charges in both engines

questions.text: What if a second rollback trigger fires, or a forward-move approval arrives, while the rollout is already in RollingBack?
questions.about: Rollback: on-call starts rollback or auto

answers.text: A declined card in resume is recorded as failed. The period stays due, so the charge is not dropped. Rollback counts the period as handled and finishes, because waiting on a declined card could hold rollback open indefinitely. Any later retry belongs to the existing billing terms. The brief does not define that retry, and the one-row-per-key ledger rule means it needs a decision, so it is an open question. A provider error or timeout is different: it is checked by key before any retry.

A rollback that started before day 35 keeps running past day 35. The 35-day clock does not stop. The rollout does not lock while RollingBack, because the lock applies only to new_only. Reprocess needs the skipped events, which age out at day 35, so a reprocess that is not finished by then cannot complete. The plan has no path for that case, so it is an open question. Until it is decided, the rollout stays RollingBack with charging frozen and on-call is paged.

A mismatch is resolved when a person marks it resolved in the rollout record with a note, and the next nightly comparison for that customer shows no mismatch. The brief does not define resolved. Who may mark it is an open question.

While charging is frozen, the nightly comparison keeps running, because it only reads invoices and writes results. The automatic trigger is ignored while the record is RollingBack. Forward moves are refused. Telling customers or Finance about delayed charges is not in the brief and the plan does not assign it, so it is an open question.

The nightly comparison job writes each night's results and the gate counters to the rollout record, in one compare-and-set. It is the only job that has the comparison data. The controller applies mode changes and runs the automatic trigger, but does not count. This replaces the earlier wording that gave counter updates to the controller.

A second rollback start or trigger during RollingBack does nothing and is logged, so starting rollback is idempotent. A forward-move approval during RollingBack is refused, because the record is in RollingBack and its version has changed. After rollback ends in old_only, a person must approve again on the current version.

questions.text: Freeze is set in the rollout record, but every mode change and nightly counter write is a compare-and-set on the record's version. If the nightly job or an approval bumps the version while rollback steps are writing, what happens to the rollback step's write?

Which invoice amount does the old engine use for periods the new engine never charged, since reprocess only writes to the shadow store with no charges?
questions.about: reprocess / resume

questions.text: Resume only charges periods whose due date has passed. What happens to periods that are not yet due when rollback ends and billing_mode becomes old_only? Does the old engine pick them up normally, and from which usage events?

questions.text: The mode diagram says 'counters reset to zero' and the text says the freeze flag is cleared and billing_mode is set in one compare-and-set. If that final write fails, what state are things in, and can charging restart before it succeeds?
questions.about: Resume: controller sets billing_mode to old_only, clears the freeze flag

questions.text: In `both`, the old engine's invoices go to the shadow store. In `shadow`, the new engine's go there. Is it one shared store with a separate partition per engine, and does the nightly job compare shadow store against the ledger?
questions.about: Shadow store

answers.text: A rollback step's write is also a compare-and-set. If the nightly job bumps the version first, the step's write fails, and the step re-reads the record. It retries only if the record is still RollingBack at that step, so it never overwrites a newer version blindly. The nightly job writes only counters, and approvals are refused during RollingBack, so neither can undo a rollback step. Added under Where the rollout state lives.

The controller moves the rollout through the five steps in order. The current step is stored in the rollout record, which the Terms already list as the rollback origin and step. A restarted controller reads that step and continues from it. The controller does not exist yet, so the scheduling is an open question.

The old engine uses the invoice it computes in reprocess for each period and writes to the shadow store. Reprocess charges nothing, but its invoices are the amounts resume charges. Periods the new engine already charged have a succeeded ledger row and are skipped. Reason: the old engine's rules applied to the same usage events give the amount it would have charged. Added to the reprocess step.

Not-yet-due periods are not on the resume list. When billing_mode becomes old_only, the old engine bills them through its normal run, from usage events it has already covered (reprocess covers the skipped events up to the time it runs). Added to resume.

A charge is in flight while its ledger intent is pending. Drain is done when no intent is pending. The freeze stops new intents, so the set only shrinks. A pending intent whose provider call timed out or errored is an unknown outcome, and drain queries it by key. A charge still awaiting its response is treated as slow. The timeout length between the two is not in the brief, so it is an open question.

This was a real gap. billing_mode is in the config service and the rollout record is separate, so one compare-and-set cannot cover both. The plan now writes billing_mode to old_only first, then makes one compare-and-set on the record that clears the freeze, clears RollingBack and resets counters. Charging stays frozen until the record write succeeds, because workers check the freeze before every charge, so charging cannot restart before success. If the record write fails, the controller retries it. The same cross-store problem affected forward moves, which now write the record first and retry billing_mode if it fails.

One shared shadow store, with a separate partition per engine, keyed by engine, customer and billing period. Yes, the nightly job compares across it and the ledger: the new engine's invoice is in the ledger or the shadow store, and the old engine's is in the other, depending on the mode. Reason: one store with partitions keeps the nightly comparison to one query. Added to the Terms and to Where the rollout state lives.

questions.text: For the shadow to both gate, where do the '7 consecutive days' count and 'mismatch rate' come from? Does the controller just read the counters the nightly job wrote, or recompute them from the comparison results?
questions.about: Forward moves, step 1 and 3: the controller works out whether the gate is met

questions.text: Starting rollback is one compare-and-set on the record. If it loses to a nightly counter write, who retries it? And between the start and the freeze flag being set, can either engine still start a new charge?

questions.text: What actually moves new_only to new_only_locked at day 35? Is it the controller, and how does it check 'no rollback in progress' and write the change?
questions.about: Mode diagram: new_only --> new_only_locked and 'day 35 reached'

questions.about: Reprocess: from the day the rollout entered new_only until reprocess runs

questions.about: Resume: periods not yet due are not on the resume list

questions.text: How does a step know it has failed rather than being slow, and how many times or how long does it retry before anyone is told? Who gets paged if a step stays stuck?
questions.about: Failure table: Any rollback step fails ... Retry the step

answers.text: The controller reads the counters the nightly job wrote. It does not recompute from comparison results. The nightly job adds one to the consecutive-day count on a matching day and resets it otherwise, so the gate reads that count. The rule is now stated in Gate counters and in forward move step 1.

Starting rollback is one CAS, and that write also sets the freeze flag. So no new charge can start once the write takes effect. A charge that passed the freeze check just before the write already has a pending ledger intent, and drain waits for it. If the start write loses to a nightly counter write, the start re-reads the record and retries, unless the record is already RollingBack. The nightly write touches only counters, so the retry is safe. Reason: this closes the window between start and freeze without adding a new mechanism. Changed: the start write now sets the freeze flag.

The controller does it. On each run, if the record is new_only, not RollingBack, and 35 or more days have passed since entering new_only, it sets the new_only_locked sub-state with a CAS. billing_mode stays new_only. Rollback start also checks the date, not only the lock, so a rollback is refused from day 35 even before the lock is written. How often the controller runs is an open question, so the check is only as prompt as its schedule. Changed: day 35 rule added, and the date check added to rollback start.

Yes. In both, the old engine already writes every invoice into the shadow store, so resume reads the old engine's invoice for the due period from there. No reprocess is needed, as the plan's both description says. A period the new engine failed to charge has no succeeded ledger row, so it is due and uncharged and goes on the resume list. Changed: resume now says where the amount comes from for origin both and for origin new_only.

Reprocess runs in passes. Each pass covers the events that arrived since the previous pass started, and it stops when a pass finds no new events. Events that arrive during freeze, drain and reconcile are covered because reprocess starts from the day the rollout entered new_only. Reason: the brief requires reprocess to finish before events age out at day 35, and a single pass would miss events that arrive during the pass. Whether passes converge is not guaranteed. A pass that never converges is a failed step and is retried, and the 35-day limit still applies. Changed: reprocess now works in passes.

Resume runs reconcile again before its final writes. Any period that became due during the rollback goes on the list and is charged by resume under the same rules, and this repeats until no due and uncharged period is left. A period that falls due after the last check is billed by the old engine's normal run once billing_mode is old_only and the freeze is cleared. Reason: resume should charge periods that fall due during rollback, not leave them to a later run. Changed: a final reconcile pass before the final write is added to resume.

A step has failed when its call returns an error. A call still running is slow, and the step keeps waiting. The brief sets no retry count and no time limit, so those are unknown. What is decided: a stuck step leaves the record in RollingBack with charging frozen, and it pages on-call, because a stuck step delays due charges. The time before paging is an open question. Changed: the failure table now says a stuck step pages on-call, and the open questions ask for the limit.

questions.text: Resume names the amount source for origin `both` and `new_only`, but not for origin `shadow`. If rollback starts from `shadow`, what does resume charge, and is there anything to do beyond the old engine's normal charging?
questions.about: Resume: amount for origin both vs origin new_only

questions.text: A declined card is recorded as failed, and that period is still due with no succeeded row. Won't the final reconcile pass list it as due and uncharged again? How does the repeat loop end, and how does it avoid charging that key a second time?
questions.about: Resume: final pass repeats until no due and uncharged period is left

questions.text: In `shadow` the old engine already charges and writes the ledger. When rollback starts there, what do drain, reconcile and resume actually do that differs from `both`? Are any periods ever on the resume list?
questions.about: Rollback / Steps: Freeze and Reconcile in origin shadow

answers.text: Origin shadow is handled in resume. In shadow the old engine already charges and writes the ledger through its normal run, so the old engine's invoice is not in the shadow store and there is no reprocess. For a period on the list, resume has the old engine compute that period's invoice from the usage events, as its normal run does, and charges that amount. The list is usually short: it holds only due periods that the normal run did not reach, for example because the freeze stopped it. Nothing else is needed beyond the old engine's normal charging path, which the freeze pauses. Reason: the shadow store does not hold the old engine's invoices in this mode, so resume must compute them.

The loop does not re-list a declined period. A decline is recorded as failed, and the list excludes any period with a succeeded or declined row. The final-pass reconcile adds only periods that became due during rollback, have no such row, and were not on an earlier list. A period on an earlier list is not re-added, and a provider error is retried inside the pass by key check, not by a new list entry. So a declined key is never charged again, and each pass adds only new periods. The loop ends when a pass adds none. Reason: without these rules the decline would be re-listed and the loop would never end.

In shadow the old engine charges through its normal run, so it already writes its invoices to the ledger. Freeze, drain and reconcile do the same job as in both: freeze pauses the old engine's charges, drain waits for its pending intents, and reconcile finds due periods with no succeeded or declined row. What differs is the amount source (computed by resume from usage events) and the list, which is usually short. Yes, periods can be on the resume list in shadow, but only due periods the normal run did not reach, for example after a freeze stopped it. The plan now says this in drain and resume.

teachbacks.text:
I'll follow one request through the whole rollout: a forward move from `shadow` to `both`, then a rollback that starts automatically from `both`. I use only the document.

1. **Nightly job feeds the gate.** The nightly job runs every night. It compares the two engines' invoices for each customer. In `shadow`, the old engine's invoice is in the billing ledger and the new engine's is in the shadow store. The shadow store is one table with a partition per engine, so the comparison is one query. A customer is a mismatch if the two totals differ by more than one cent. A day matches if its mismatch rate is under 0.1 percent and at least 5,000 invoices were compared that day. On a matching day the job adds one to the consecutive-day count. On any other day, including a night when the comparison fails or doesn't run, it resets the count to zero. It writes the night's results and the gate counters to the rollout record in one CAS. It only counts and never changes the mode.

2. **Controller reads the record.** The controller reads the rollout record and the counters. It does not recount invoices. Once the count reaches 7 consecutive matching days, the gate is met.

3. **A person approves.** A person approves the move to `both`. The approval names the record version they saw.

4. **Controller checks and applies.** The controller checks three things: the gate is met, the version is still current, and the record is not `RollingBack`. If any check fails, the move is refused and nothing changes. If all pass, it writes the new mode into the rollout record with a CAS. Then it sets `billing_mode` to `both`. If the record write fails, the mode stays the same and the person approves again on the current version. If the `billing_mode` write fails, the controller retries it, and workers keep the old mode until it succeeds.

5. **Running in `both`.** The new engine charges. It writes a ledger intent (key = customer plus billing period, status pending), then charges the provider using that same key as the idempotency key, then records the result as succeeded or failed. The ledger allows one row per key. Its invoice goes in the ledger. The old engine keeps computing every invoice into the shadow store without charging. Mismatches don't trigger a rollback. They block the later move to `new_only` until a person marks them resolved and the next nightly comparison shows no mismatch for that customer.

6. **Automatic trigger.** The controller sees the new engine's charge failure rate go above 2 percent in some 10-minute window. In `both`, this is allowed at any time. It starts rollback and pages on-call. (On-call can also start rollback by hand from `shadow`, `both`, or `new_only` before day 35.)

7. **Start write.** The start is one CAS on the record. In that single write it saves the origin (`both`), sets `RollingBack`, and sets the freeze flag. If it loses a version race, it re-reads the record and retries, unless the record is already `RollingBack`. In that case a second start does nothing and is logged. If the freeze flag can't be set, it retries and does not start drain. `billing_mode` stays `both` until the final writes. The controller stores its current step in the record, so a restarted controller continues from there.

8. **Freeze.** Both engines check the freeze flag before each charge, so no new charge begins. The new engine stops writing to the ledger. The freeze lasts until the final writes.

9. **Drain.** Drain waits until no ledger intent is pending. A charge that passed the freeze check just before the start write already has a pending intent, so drain waits for it. Freeze stops new charges, so the set of pending intents only shrinks. For each pending intent: if it is still waiting on the provider, it is slow and drain keeps waiting. If the provider call timed out or errored, the outcome is unknown, so drain asks the provider about that key and never resends without checking. If the provider can't answer, drain stays in this step. State lives in the ledger intents.

10. **Reconcile.** For each customer and period: a succeeded ledger row means it is charged, so leave it. An intent with no result gets a provider check by key. If the provider shows a charge, record it as succeeded. If not, the period is uncharged. A due and uncharged period (due date passed under existing billing terms, no succeeded row) goes on the resume list. A declined row does not go on the list. If the provider can't answer, reconcile stays in this step. State lives in the ledger. This step also covers the case where a charge succeeded but recording the result failed. The intent stayed pending, and reconcile fixes it by asking the provider.

11. **Reprocess.** The origin is `both`, so this step is skipped. (If the origin were `new_only`, the old engine would recompute the usage events it skipped since entering `new_only`, into the shadow store without charging. It would work in passes until a pass finds no new events, and retry on failure. It must finish before the events age out at 35 days.)

12. **Resume.** The old engine charges each period on the list. With origin `both`, the amount is the old engine's invoice already in the shadow store. For each period it writes the ledger intent first, then charges with the key, then records the result. If the intent write fails, it does not charge. A period that already has a succeeded row is skipped, which is checked on the row, not the amount. A declined card is recorded as failed. The period stays due, but rollback counts it as handled and does not retry it. A provider error or timeout is checked by key before any retry, and the retry reuses the same key. Periods not yet due are left for the old engine's normal run after rollback.

13. **Final pass.** Before the final writes, resume runs reconcile again. It adds only periods that became due during rollback, have no succeeded or declined row, and aren't already on an earlier list. It charges them as above and repeats until a pass adds nothing.

14. **Final writes.** First it sets `billing_mode` to `old_only`. Then it makes one CAS on the record that clears the freeze flag, `RollingBack`, the origin and the step, and zeroes the gate counters. Charging stays frozen until the record write succeeds. If either write fails, charging stays frozen and the write is retried.

15. **Afterwards.** The system is in `old_only`. The old engine bills anything that falls due later through its normal run. To get back to `shadow`, a person must approve again on the current record version, and the 7-day count starts from zero.

16. **Failure in any rollback step.** The rollout stays in `RollingBack` with charging frozen, the step is retried, and a stuck step pages on-call.

**Side rule, day 35.** While in `new_only`, once 35 days have passed since entering it, the controller sets `new_only_locked` in the record (and `billing_mode` stays `new_only`). From then on rollback is refused. The rollback start also checks the date, so it refuses even before the lock is written. The automatic trigger still pages on-call but doesn't roll back.
gaps: The document does not say who or what actually runs the controller or how often, so I can't say when the automatic trigger or the day-35 check fires. It lists this as an open question.
It does not define what counts as a charge failure (declined card versus provider error) or where the failure-rate data comes from, so I can't say how the trigger measures the 2 percent rate.
It does not say how workers learn the freeze flag is set. The flag is described as a proposal, and how the engines read it before each charge is not defined.
It does not say how long a charge may stay pending before drain treats it as unknown. Drain can wait indefinitely, and it does not say how long a step may retry before on-call is paged.
The fields of the ledger intent row are not defined. It is also unclear how a ledger with one row per key records a declined attempt and a later retry.
It does not say whether a person who approves a move, or who marks a mismatch resolved, uses any particular interface. It also does not say who approves.

It does not say what happens to a rollback still running on day 35 when the origin is `new_only`. The record stays frozen and on-call is paged, but there is no path forward. This is the one gap that falls on the `new_only` flow, so I did not trace that flow.
It does not say whether the shadow store is kept or cleared after rollback.
It does not say how a freeze affects customers' due charges. There is no limit on freeze duration and no named owner for notifying customers and Finance.
It does not say where the rollout record physically lives. It says to decide this before the controller is written.

It does not say how the nightly job gets the old engine's invoice in `new_only`. It does not say how the controller, which writes the lock and trigger, learns the date of entering `new_only` beyond that being a record field.
